Skill: Model debugging and integration

> Teoría:   

+ Desplegar un modelo de ML entrenado:
  - Recordatorio de que para desplegar un modelo debe definirse un flujo y establecer un pipeline.
  - ¿Cómo desplegar el modelo? Principales aspectos a tener en cuenta para ponerlo en producción.
  - Formas de consumir el modelo
    -- Emplearlo en procesamiento por lotes
    -- Invocarlo en un backend (APIs)
  - Cómo integrar el modelo dentro de un pipeline de Prefect

+ Monitoreo de salud de un modelo
   - ¿Por qué es importante monitorear a un modelo?
   - Track health, quality, freshness, and failures.
   - Métricas comunes con Prefect
     -- Runs completadas / fallos → Prefect registra el estado de cada ejecución en su base de datos interna.
     -- Duración media → diferencia entre start_time y end_time de cada run.
     -- Filas cargadas → esto sí requiere que tú lo registres explícitamente, por ejemplo con return len(df) en load() o usando prefect.context / artefactos.
   - ¿Qué debe mostrar un dashboard de monitorización de un modelo?
How to think:
- Real datasets produce real problems — overfitting, imbalanced classes, poor generalization. 
- It's necessary to have a systematic way to diagnose and fix, not just re-run, hoping for better results.
Best practices:
- Serialize the full pipeline (preprocessing + model), not just the model weights — use joblib
- Version every deployed artifact — model file, preprocessing config, and training data snapshot
- Expose the model via a typed API contract — define input schema and output schema explicitly
- Separate batch and online serving paths — they have different latency, throughput, and failure profiles
- Gate deployment with a minimum performance threshold — never deploy a model without a quality bar
Anti pattern:
- Deploying only the model without the scaler/encoder → prediction pipeline breaks silently
- No versioning → impossible to roll back when a new model degrades
- Running batch inference inside a web request → blocks the API, wrong tool for the job
- Hardcoding preprocessing logic in the serving layer separately from training → train/serve skew

> Teoría:

    - ¿Cómo funciona una bd vectorial?

  + Using Qdrant
    - ¿Qué es Qdrant?
    - Core Qdrant concepts overview (with analogies, avoiding too technical-mathematical explanations)
      -- Collections — the equivalent of a table; stores vectors of a fixed dimension with a distance metric (cosine, dot product, Euclidean)
      -- Points — a record: {id, vector, payload}; payload is arbitrary JSON metadata
      -- Vectors — Qdrant supports dense vectors for semantic similarity, sparse vectors for full-text/keyword search, and multivectors for late-interaction models like ColBERT 
      -- Why is Qdrant fast? (Very simple overview of HNSW index — Qdrant uses Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs for efficient ANN search with low latency and high recall)
    - Basic operations (hands-on)
      -- Create a collection with the right vector size and distance metric
      -- Upsert points (insert/update)
      -- Query: search() with a vector → get top-K similar results
      -- Filter by payload during search (this is a key differentiator vs. FAISS)
      -- Delete points; update payload

  + Chunking y Embedding
    - ¿Qué es el chunking?
    - ¿Qué es el embedding?
    - Proceso:
      1. Elegir cómo hacer chunking
      2. Elegir a qué hacer embedding
      3. Elegir el modelo (que no es lo mismo que el LLM) para realizar el embedding.

    - Comparativa de modelos de embeddings: https://www.awesomescreenshot.com/image/60606596?key=384f6e1ebdb4bf252167e9dd7518576c
How to think:
- Cuándo es necesario un RAG
- Por qué RAG no debe ser precisamente considerado una Memoria, sino una base de conocimiento
- Cómo afecta el tamaño de mis chunks a un RAG
-
Best practices:
- Dejar que el LLM sintetice los embeddings para obtener el mejor resultado, en lugar de seleccionar el aparentemente "mejor".
- Siempre decirle a la IA cómo usar los chunks
- Siempre decirle a la IA que diga que no sabe algo para evitar improvisaciones y alucinaciones.
- Mantener la cantidad de chunks baja y de buena calidad para evitar "lost in the middle".

- Chunk documents by semantic unit (section, paragraph), not by fixed character count
- Store both the chunk and its source metadata (doc ID, page, section title) in the vector store
- Use a retrieval step that returns k candidates, then rerank before passing to the LLM
- Set a similarity threshold — discard chunks below it rather than always forcing k results
- Keep the retrieval pipeline and the generation prompt decoupled — they evolve at different rates
- Evaluate retrieval and generation separately; a bad answer can fail at either layer
- Embed at query time with the same model used at indexing time — never mix embedding models
- Log retrieved chunks alongside the final answer for debugging and audit
Patterns:
- Chunking with overlap — small overlap between adjacent chunks prevents context loss at boundaries
- Hybrid search — combine dense (vector) + sparse (BM25/keyword) retrieval, then merge results
- Metadata filtering — pre-filter by date, category, or source before vector search to reduce noise
- Prompt stuffing with source attribution — include chunk source in the context block so the LLM can cite it
- Re-ranking — use a cross-encoder or LLM-based reranker to reorder the top-k before generation
- Parent-child chunking — index small chunks for precision retrieval, expand to parent chunk for context
- Query expansion — rephrase or expand the user query before retrieval to improve recall
Anti pattern:
- Chunks muy grandes o muy pequeños
- No respetar los límites naturales del contenido (dejar la mitad de un párrafo en un chunk y la otra en otro)
- No limpiar el contenido
- No incluir el contexto del chunk. (Un chunk que dice "como vimos anteriormente" pero el chunk no sabe qué había anteriormente.
- Embedding de preguntas junto con respuestas
- No filtrar por metadatos. No puedes usar solo los embeddings. (Una función se explica igual pero se escribe distinto en JS y Python)
- Confiar ciegamente en el top-1 de similitud. El mejor contexto puede estar en el segundo o tercero.
- No poner un puntaje mínimo de similaridad (Threshold demasiado bajo)
- No instruir al LLM sobre cómo usar el contexto.

### AGENTIC ENGINEERING ###
Skill: Building an AI Agent capable of calling tools (functions)

The customer support AI Agent will be able to fetch company information and respond in real time.

+ Conceptos fundamentales en Ingeniería Agéntica
  - ¿Qué es un agente?
  - estado (state)
  - nodo (node)
  - dirección (edge)
  - compilación (compile)
  - checkpointing
  - tool
  - interruption
  - yield
  - loop
  - trace
  - evals
  - fitness
  - ¿En qué consiste la ingeniería de agentes?

+ Elementos fundamentales en configuración de la Ingeniería Agéntica
  - ¿Componentes principales de un agente?
    -- Modelo (LLM) / Conexión a una LLM API
    -- System prompt
    -- Temperature
  - Understanding the agentic loop: prompt → model response → tool call detected → execute function → feed result back → next model response
    -- How to detect a tool call in the response (tool_use block / finish_reason: tool_calls)
    -- How to format tool results and re-inject them into the conversation history
  - Minimum viable sequence:
   -- Call a single tool manually (hardcoded) → understand the schema
   -- Let the model decide when to call it (1 tool, 1 turn)
   -- Build the loop (multi-turn, 1 tool)
   -- Expand to multiple tools (routing logic)
   -- Add error handling and stopping conditions 

+ Introducción a LangGraph:
  - ¿Qué es y para qué sirve LangGraph?
  - Ejemplo de un agente ingenuo (Agent loop básico en Python sin LangGraph)
  - Crear un agente básico con LangGraph
How to think:
- ¿Qué diferencia a un agente de un chat?
- ¿Por qué un agente debe tener responsabilidades específicas y no ser un "todero"?
- ¿cómo funciona un ciclo de agente? prompt → model response → tool call detected → execute function → feed result back → next model response
Best practices:
- Treat the LLM as one component inside a larger system — it decides, the system executes
- Keep state minimal and explicit — only what the agent needs to make the next decision
- Define edges based on output conditions, not hardcoded sequences
- Implement checkpointing at every meaningful state transition — never at arbitrary intervals
- Add evals and fitness checks as first-class steps in the graph, not afterthoughts

- Every tool must have a typed input/output contract — the LLM cannot reason about ambiguous interfaces
- Handle tool failure explicitly in the graph — define a failure edge, not just a success path
- Make every tool idempotent — the agent will retry
- Set timeouts on every tool call — an unresponsive tool stalls the entire loop

- Compile the graph before any execution — catch structural errors at build time, not runtime
- Use yield for streaming intermediate outputs — never make the user wait for full completion
- Design graphs so every node has a single clear responsibility — mirrors the Narrow Tool Pattern
- Keep system prompt and graph architecture aligned — ambiguity in one amplifies ambiguity in the other
Patterns:
- State Machine Pattern — model agent behavior as explicit states + transitions, not free-form loops
- Tool Registry Pattern — register tools declaratively; the LLM selects, the runtime executes
- Interrupt-and-Resume Pattern — pause graph execution to collect human input, then resume from checkpoint
- Trace-and-Eval Pattern — every run produces a trace; evals run against the trace, not live execution

- Fallback Edge Pattern — on tool failure, route to a recovery node (retry, clarify, or escalate) rather than crashing
- Human-in-the-Loop Pattern — use interrupt to pause and yield control to the user when the agent reaches ambiguity it cannot resolve autonomously
- Narrow Tool Pattern — one tool, one responsibility; composability beats multi-purpose tools

- Naive Agent → Structured Graph Migration Pattern — start with a raw Python loop to understand the problem, then formalize as a LangGraph state machine
- Subgraph Pattern — encapsulate complex multi-step behavior (e.g., retrieval + rerank + respond) as a nested graph, callable as a single node
- Conditional Edge Pattern — route graph execution based on structured output from the LLM (e.g., {action: "escalate" | "respond" | "clarify"})
Anti pattern:
- Esperar precisión absoluta del LLM: Los agentes deben diseñarse para tolerar errores del modelo.
- Letting the LLM control the loop directly — it should signal intent, not drive execution
- Storing full conversation history in state — summarize or window it; unbounded state kills performance
- No checkpointing → process crash = full restart from zero
- Hardcoding edge conditions as prompt instructions instead of graph logic — the architecture must enforce constraints, not the prompt

- Tools with side effects that aren't idempotent — retries cause duplicate actions (emails sent twice, records created twice)
- No failure path in the graph → unhandled tool errors propagate as LLM context noise
- Passing raw tool errors to the LLM without sanitizing — leaks internals, confuses reasoning
- Tools that do too much — the LLM can't accurately predict behavior, leading to wrong calls

- Building directly in LangGraph without first understanding the naive loop — abstractions hide bugs when fundamentals are unclear
- Monolithic single-node graphs — no observability, no retry granularity, no extensibility
- Extending behavior by modifying the prompt instead of the graph — prompt-only architecture breaks as complexity grows
- No trace instrumentation → debugging agentic failures without traces is guesswork

Skill: Dotar de memoria a un agente

> Teoría:
+ Memoria para agentes:
  - ¿Qué es la memoria de un agente inteligente?
  - ¿Por qué es importante la memoria?
  - ¿Cómo organizar la memoria de una gente?
  - Errores más comunes al implementar la memoria de un agente
  - Mejores prácticas en la creación de memoria de agentes

+ Arquitecturas de memoria:
  - Ventana de contexto (texto sin estado): la tarea cabe en una sesión y no requiere persistencia
  - Memoria externa (VectorDBs, RAGs): para buscar por similaridad semántica o si el contexto es muy grande
  - Knowledge graphs (GraphRAG, neo4j): para memoria con relaciones explícitas (dependencia, jerarquía, causalidad)
  - Memoria episódica (Prompt caching, Redis, key-value): Cuando el agente debe conocer su historial y personalizar. 
  - Memoria en parámetros: Conocimiento estable y vale la pena reentrenar (fine-tuning) el modelo. Superficial y con referencia a que fine-tuning es una práctica muy costosa y por tanto en cierto desuso.
  - Self-improving memory: Mecanismos para que la memoria se mantenga por sí sola.
How to think:
- ¿Cuándo es necesaria la memoria?
- Comprender el tipo de memoria según el caso de uso.
Best practices:
- Define what the agent must remember, for how long, and why before choosing an architecture
- Separate memory by temporal scope: within-session (context window), across-session (external store), permanent (parameters)
- Design memory as a first-class system component — not an afterthought bolted onto the prompt
- Make memory reads and writes explicit in the graph — agents should not implicitly accumulate state

- Use context window only when the full task fits in one session and persistence is not required
- Use VectorDB / RAG when retrieval is semantic and the corpus is too large for the context window
- Use Knowledge Graphs when relationships between entities matter — dependency, hierarchy, causality — not just similarity
- Use episodic memory (Redis, key-value, prompt caching) when the agent must personalize based on interaction history
- Treat parametric memory (fine-tuning) as a last resort — it is expensive, slow to update, and encodes knowledge that cannot be selectively forgotten
- Implement self-improving memory with a cleanup and consolidation cycle — raw memory accumulation without curation degrades retrieval quality over time
Patterns:
- Memory Taxonomy Pattern — classify every piece of information the agent needs into: ephemeral / episodic / semantic / parametric before implementation
- Explicit Memory Interface Pattern — memory is accessed through typed read/write operations, not by stuffing everything into the system prompt

- Tiered Memory Pattern — context window for immediate task, episodic store for session history, VectorDB for knowledge retrieval; route queries to the appropriate tier
RAG-as-Working-Memory Pattern — retrieve only the relevant chunks per query; never load the full knowledge base into context
- GraphRAG Pattern — use knowledge graph traversal to retrieve relational context that vector similarity cannot capture (e.g., "what depends on X")
- Memory Consolidation Pattern — periodically summarize and compress episodic memory; discard low-relevance entries to prevent retrieval noise
Anti pattern:
- Appending the full conversation history to every prompt — context bloat degrades reasoning and increases cost linearly
- Choosing a memory architecture before defining the retrieval requirement — architecture must follow access pattern, not preference
- Treating memory as a single unified store — different scopes require different backends

- Using a VectorDB when relationships between entities are the actual retrieval requirement — cosine similarity is blind to structure
- Fine-tuning to add recent or frequently changing knowledge — use RAG instead; fine-tuning is for stable behavioral patterns, not factual updates
- No eviction or consolidation policy on episodic memory → unbounded growth, degraded retrieval precision over time
- Self-improving memory with no human review gate → the agent reinforces its own errors autonomously

Skill: Implementar sistemas seguros de orquestación de agentes

> Teoría:

  + Harnesss Engineering
    - Agent = Model + Harness — (el modelo decide, el harness ejecuta, orquesta herramientas y mantiene estado). 
    - El harness es todo lo que envuelve al modelo (orquestación de tools, loops de verificación, contexto/memoria, guardrails y observabilidad) para convertir la inteligencia cruda del modelo en un agente confiable y accionable
    - Cinco capas del harness de producción (referencial, poca profundidad): orquestación de tools, loops de verificación, contexto y memoria, guardrails, y observabilidad
    - ¿Por qué el Harness es importante?
      -- Caso de evidencia: En marzo de 2026, el equipo de LangChain subió su agente de codificación del puesto 30 al puesto 5 en Terminal Bench 2.0 sin cambiar el modelo subyacente — la mejora vino enteramente de optimizar el harness.

  + Guardrails
    - ¿Qué son los Guardrails o Guardarraíles?
    - ¿Por qué es necesario aplicar guardrails?
    - Los tres tipos de fallo que justifican guardrails: fallos estructurales (JSON malformado, campos faltantes), fallos de contenido (alucinaciones, fuga de PII, contenido dañino) y fallos de seguridad (inyección de prompt que manipula al modelo para ignorar instrucciones o exfiltrar datos)
    - Ejemplos de casos de la vida real más conocidos en los que aplicar de Guardrails
    - Mejores prácticas en guardrails
How to think:
- Por qué un agente necesita guardrails y un chatbot simple no tanto (el agente actúa, no solo responde)
- ¿Cómo evito que mis visitas usen mi agente como un ChatGPT libre? -> Guardrails 
- ¿Cómo logro que mis agentes estén optimizados por caso de uso? (contexto, tools, modelos, memoria, evals)
- Una vez optimizados mis agentes, hay que orquestarlos -> Harness
- Cada tipo de fallo (estructural, de contenido, de seguridad/inyección) requiere estrategias y herramientas distintas.
- ¿por qué un solo guardrail nunca es suficiente?

- El principio fundacional del harnessing (mentalidad, no herramienta): "Cada vez que un agente comete un error, se toma el tiempo de diseñar una solución para que el agente nunca vuelva a cometer ese error" — la mayoría de las veces esa solución es un harness mejorado, no un modelo mejor.
Best practices:
- separar instrucciones del sistema de input del usuario
- sanitizar inputs 
- nunca confiar en texto que viene de una tool externa (web, documento) como si fueran instrucciones del sistema.
Patterns:
- Guardrails (Restricciones para evitar comportamientos inesperados. Ejemplos: límite de iteraciones, validación de argumentos, whitelist de tools)

- Fallback (Si una tool falla: intentar alternativa responder parcialmente pedir clarificación)

- Human-in-the-loop para acciones irreversibles
Anti pattern:
- Creer que "no hagas nada inseguro" protege al agente
- Crear un único filtro de protección.
- Multiagente cuando un solo agente bien diseñado bastaba (over-engineering).
- Falta de contrato claro entre agentes (inputs/outputs no tipados).
- Ausencia de mecanismo de terminación o resolución de desacuerdos entre agentes.

### AGENTIC WORKFLOWS ###
Skill: Implement multi-agent systems to solve complex problems

> Teoría:

+ Introducción a sistemas multiagente:
  - ¿Qué significa que un sistema sea multiagente?
  - ¿Qué es la orquestación de agentes?
  - Workflows and agentic systems are based on LLMs and the various augmentations you add to them. Tool calling, structured outputs, and short-term memory are a few options for tailoring LLMs to your needs.
  - Importancia de los roles y especialización: agentes con propósitos acotados (planificador, ejecutor, verificador, orquestador) en lugar de un agente "todólogo".
  - Diferencia entre un agente único y un sistema multiagente
   
+ Orchestrating a multi-agent system in LangGraph
  - What is an agent workflow
    -- LLM is embedded in predefined code paths
    -- LLM directs control flow through predefined code paths
  - Referencia breve a los patrones de flujo que se verán en Learnpacks aparte (basada en https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/workflows-agents):
    -- Pipeline secuencial (Prompt chaining)
    -- Parallelization
    -- Routing
    -- Orchestrator-worker pattern (include the difference with routing)
    -- Evaluator-optimizer
  - ToolNode como evolución del ToolCalling en agentic workflows: replace manual tool dispatch logic with a ToolNode; tools read from and write to graph state directly
  - Access graph state and context from tools

+ Comunicación y estado en sistemas multiagente:
  - Paso de mensajes vs. memoria compartida: cómo los agentes intercambian contexto (mensajes estructurados, blackboard/estado compartido).
  - Formato de los mensajes: JSON estructurado vs. lenguaje natural libre, y por qué la estructura reduce errores de interpretación entre agentes.
  - Gestión de contexto: cada agente no necesita ver todo el historial; hay que diseñar qué contexto recibe cada uno.

+ Agentic workflow patterns: Router pattern (https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/workflows-agents#routing)
  - Implementing the routing pattern in LangGraph
  - Ejemplos de casos reales en los que se aplica el patrón

+ Agentic workflow patterns: Orchestrator-worker pattern (https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/workflows-agents#orchestrator-worker)
  - Why an Orchestrator
  - Why Workers
  - Why a Synthesizer
  - Creating workers in LangGraph
  - Implementing an orchestrator-worker-synthetizer in LangGraph
  - Ejemplos de casos reales en los que se aplica el patrón
How to think:
- ¿Cuándo un solo agente con buenas herramientas es suficiente vs. cuándo conviene dividir responsabilidades entre varios.?
- Saber determinar la estrategia adecuada según cada problema
- Los agentes requieren de una comunicación clara para que el flujo sea exitoso
- Routing vs Orchestration
- Roles y responsabilidades claras y acotadas
Best practices:
- Assign one purpose per agent — planner, executor, verifier, orchestrator; never a generalist agent
- Define explicit interfaces between agents — what goes in, what comes out, typed and documented
- Design agents so they are replaceable — swapping one agent should not require rewriting the others
- Keep the orchestrator stateless with respect to task logic — it routes and delegates, it does not execute

- Use prompt chaining when steps are strictly sequential and each output feeds the next — simplest, most debuggable
- Use parallelization only when subtasks are truly independent — don't parallelize for speed if outputs are interdependent
- Use routing when the workflow path depends on the content of the LLM output — the LLM classifies, the graph routes
- Prefer ToolNode over raw tool-calling loops — it handles tool dispatch, error capture, and state update consistently
- Give each agent access to only the state slice it needs — not the full graph context

- Use structured JSON messages between agents — free-form natural language between agents compounds errors at every hop
- Design per-agent context windows explicitly — each agent receives only the state it needs to make its decision
- Use a shared blackboard (graph state) for coordination data; use message passing for task handoffs
- Version the message schema — agents evolve independently; schema mismatches must be caught at the boundary
Patterns:
- Orquestador-trabajador (orchestrator-worker): un agente central delega subtareas a agentes especializados.
- Pipeline secuencial: salida de un agente alimenta al siguiente (útil para flujos tipo ETL de contenido/razonamiento).
- Router: un agente clasifica la tarea y decide a qué agente/herramienta enviarla.

- Role Specialization Pattern — each agent owns a bounded capability; compose agents to cover the full workflow
- Orchestrator-Worker-Synthesizer Pattern — orchestrator decomposes the task, workers execute in parallel, synthesizer merges results

- Blackboard Pattern — agents read/write to a shared state object; the orchestrator controls write access to prevent conflicts
- Scoped Context Pattern — before invoking each agent, project the full state down to the minimal context that agent requires
- Structured Handoff Pattern — task delegation is a typed message ({task, inputs, expected_output_schema}), not a natural language instruction
Anti pattern:
- Agentes ciegos, sin saber el estado del fluj
- Building a single "todólogo" agent and adding tools until it breaks — complexity without structure
- Orchestrator that executes domain logic — it becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure
- Agents without defined output schemas — downstream agents receive ambiguous input and hallucinate interpretations
- Using routing where orchestrator-worker is needed — routing selects one path; orchestrator-worker decomposes into parallel tasks; they are not interchangeable
- Parallelizing agents that share mutable state — race conditions corrupt the graph state
- Accessing full conversation history from every tool — tools should read only the state keys they declare as dependencies
- Passing full conversation history to every agent — context bloat degrades reasoning quality and increases latency
- Free-form natural language as the inter-agent protocol — ambiguity compounds across hops; one misinterpretation cascades
- No message schema versioning — a change in one agent's output silently breaks all downstream agents
- Shared mutable state with no access control — multiple agents writing to the same key without coordination corrupts state

Skill: Implement multi-agent systems that have control and resuming systems

> Teoría:

+ Control de sistemas multiagentes
  - Guardrails: validación de salidas antes de pasarlas al siguiente agente (evitar la propagación de errores en cascada).
  - Límites de iteración/loops: evitar bucles infinitos entre agentes que se corrigen mutuamente sin converger.
  - Trazabilidad: poder ver qué agente hizo qué, con qué input/output (esencial para debugging, ya que los fallos multiagente son más difíciles de rastrear que en un solo agente).
  - Costos y latencia: cada agente adicional multiplica las llamadas al modelo; hay que enseñar el trade-off entre complejidad y costo.
  - Arbitration

+ Checkpointing and interruptions
  - Checkpointing and interruptions como implementación técnica del Human-in-the-loop mediante puntos de control donde un humano aprueba antes de continuar.
    -- implementación técnica: interrupt + checkpointer + resume
  - Checkpointing
    -- Qué es: persistencia del state del grafo en puntos determinados de la ejecución.
    -- Por qué importa: reanudación tras fallo, human-in-the-loop, debugging/time-travel.
    -- Mecanismo en LangGraph: checkpointer (memoria, SQLite, Postgres) + thread_id para identificar ejecuciones independientes.
  - Interruptions
    -- Qué es: pausa explícita de la ejecución antes de un nodo crítico o irreversible.
    -- Relación con checkpointing: la interrupción solo es útil porque el estado quedó persistido — sin checkpoint, no hay "dónde" reanudar.
    -- Distinción clave a remarcar: interrupción = feature (pausar para aprobación humana); checkpointing = infraestructura (que hace posible reanudar exactamente donde se pausó).
  - Importancia de implementar bien el "resume".
How to think: - Comprender el trade-off entre complejidad y costo
Best practices:
- Validate every inter-agent output before passing it downstream — schema, type, and domain constraints
- Fail fast and explicitly at the boundary — a rejected output must return a typed error, not null or a warning
- Design guardrails as separate nodes, not inline prompt instructions — the graph enforces constraints, not the model
- Define the acceptable output envelope per agent during design, not after the first failure

- Set a max_iterations hard ceiling on every loop — never rely solely on convergence conditions
- Define arbitration rules before deployment — what happens when two agents produce conflicting outputs
- Track iteration count as an explicit state key — makes loop limits a trivial conditional edge
- Assign a designated arbitrator node for conflicts — do not let agents resolve disagreements among themselves

- Log agent_id, input, output, timestamp, and iteration on every node execution
- Treat trace data as a first-class artifact — store it, version it, query it
- Account for cost per agent call at design time — every additional agent multiplies model invocations
- Profile latency per node before scaling — identify the bottleneck agent before adding parallelism

- Checkpoint at every meaningful state transition — before irreversible actions, after expensive computations
- Use thread_id to isolate independent executions — never share a checkpoint store across unrelated runs without namespacing
- Choose the checkpointer backend by durability requirement: in-memory for dev, SQLite for single-node, Postgres for production
- Treat the checkpoint as the source of truth for resume — never reconstruct state from logs

- Treat interruption and checkpointing as a pair — an interruption without a checkpoint has nowhere to resume from
- Place interruptions before critical or irreversible nodes — not after
- Implement resume as an explicit graph entry point — not a retry of the full flow from the start
- Validate human input on resume before re-entering the graph — treat it as untrusted external input
Patterns:
- Boundary Validation Pattern — insert a lightweight validator node between every producer and consumer agent; it passes or blocks, never transforms
- Error Propagation Firewall Pattern — on validation failure, route to a recovery node; never forward a malformed output to the next agent

- Hard Stop Pattern — conditional edge checks iteration >= max_iterations before re-entering the loop; routes to synthesizer or failure handler
- Arbitration Node Pattern — dedicated node receives conflicting outputs with their scores and applies a deterministic resolution rule (highest score, human escalation, or domain rule)

- Trace-as-State Pattern — append a trace entry to graph state on every node execution; the full execution history travels with the run
- Cost Budget Pattern — define a max token/call budget per flow; the orchestrator checks remaining budget before delegating to a new agent

- Pre-Irreversible-Action Checkpoint Pattern — always checkpoint immediately before any node that sends an email, writes to a database, or calls an external API
- Time-Travel Debug Pattern — use checkpoints to replay execution from any prior state; essential for diagnosing multi-agent failures

- Interrupt-Checkpoint-Resume Pattern — interrupt signals pause → checkpointer persists state → human provides input → graph resumes from the exact checkpoint with the new input injected into state
- Approval Gate Pattern — wrap any irreversible action in an interrupt; the action node only executes after explicit human approval is recorded in state
Anti pattern:
- No versionar ni limpiar checkpoints (crecimiento descontrolado de almacenamiento).
Interrumpir sin haber configurado checkpointer (la pausa no es reanudable, se pierde el estado).
- Usar interrupciones como sustituto de guardrails automáticos — la interrupción es para juicio humano en decisiones ambiguas, no para validaciones que un guardrail debería resolver solo.

- Trusting that the upstream agent produced valid output — validate always, regardless of agent source
- Embedding validation logic in the consuming agent's prompt — downstream agents should not compensate for upstream failures
- Silent failure on invalid output → malformed data propagates, error surfaces three hops later with no traceable origin

- Two agents that mutually correct each other with no convergence criterion → infinite loop
- Arbitration logic embedded in an LLM prompt — non-deterministic, untestable, not auditable
- No iteration counter in state → loop limit cannot be enforced by the graph

- No per-agent logging → multi-agent failures are untraceable; you see the final wrong output with no path to the cause
- Adding agents to improve quality without measuring cost impact — complexity has a compounding cost
- Assuming parallelism reduces cost — it reduces latency, not token consumption

- Checkpointing only at the end of the flow → crash mid-execution = full restart
- Using in-memory checkpointer in production → state lost on process restart
- No thread_id namespacing → concurrent runs corrupt each other's checkpoints

- Interrupting without checkpointing → state is lost; resume is impossible without replaying the full flow
- Resume that restarts the flow from node 0 — defeats the purpose of checkpointing entirely
- Skipping input validation on resume → a human can inject malformed state that corrupts the rest of the graph

### REAL-TIME COMMUNICATION ###
Skill: Implementar sistemas de tiempo real con conexiones unidireccionales

> Teoría:
 + Comunicación en tiempo real
   - ¿Por qué es necesaria la comunicación en tiempo real?
   - ¿Qué significa que sea en tiempo real?
   - ¿Por qué no basta con request/response tradicional (HTTP clásico)?
     -- Casos que lo exigen: chat, notificaciones live, streaming de LLM, colaboración multiusuario, agentes que necesitan ser interrumpidos. 
   - Breve referencia a los modelos de comunicación: 
     -- Polling / long-polling → Lo que siempre se ha hecho con fetch.
     -- HTTP Streaming (chunked transfer encoding) ← el servidor mantiene la conexión abierta y envía la respuesta en fragmentos (Transfer-Encoding: chunked), en lugar de esperar a tener el body completo.
        - Por qué importa: es el mecanismo de bajo nivel que hace posible todo lo demás — cuando el estudiante ve response.body.getReader() en JS o itera un stream en Python, está tocando esto directamente.
     -- SSE (unidireccional servidor→cliente) → el caso más simple de "push" real.
     -- WebSockets (bidireccional) → cuando el cliente también necesita hablar.
   - Tabla comparativa de los modelos de comunicación: dirección, complejidad, overhead, caso de uso típico.

  + Errores comunes y buenas prácticas en comunicaciones en tiempo real
    - Reconexión y backoff.
    - Backpressure.
    - Nombramiento de eventos y diseño de payloads.
    - Idempotencia en entrega de mensajes.

  + Transmisión de datos: Streaming vs Batch
    - ¿Qué es batch?
    - ¿Qué es streaming?
    - Streaming vs Batch
    - Cómo se implementa streaming en Python con yield
    - Streaming modes de LangGraph (values, updates, messages, custom): cómo LangGraph expone distintos "niveles" de eventos.

  + Server-Sent Events:
    - conexión unidireccional servidor→cliente sobre HTTP
    - Es el mecanismo detrás del streaming de tokens de OpenAI/Anthropic/etc. 
    - Es, literalmente, como llega la respuesta de un LLM token por token a la UI.
How to think:
- Consumir un stream de LLM con SSE en un cliente (fetch + ReadableStream, o librería del SDK).
- Choose the communication model based on directionality and latency requirement — not familiarity
- Use HTTP Streaming when you control both ends and need the simplest possible server-push without a protocol upgrade
- Use SSE when the server pushes a stream and the client only listens — LLM token streaming, notifications
- Avoid polling in new systems — use it only when SSE/WebSockets are explicitly unavailable in the target environment
Best practices:
- Always set Content-Type: text/event-stream and Cache-Control: no-cache — missing either breaks SSE in most clients
- Use named events (event: token, event: error, event: done) — unnamed data: streams are untyped and hard to evolve
- Send a heartbeat event on a fixed interval — prevents proxies and load balancers from closing idle connections
- Terminate the stream with an explicit [DONE] event — the client must know when the stream ends, not infer it from silence
- Use namespaced, verb-noun event names — agent.tool_called, llm.token_received, task.completed
- Keep payloads minimal and typed — include only what the consumer needs to act; no internal state leakage
Patterns:
- idempotencia y control de "at-least-once delivery" cuando el canal en tiempo real se combina con colas de mensajes.
- Protocol Selection Matrix Pattern — map (directionality × persistence × complexity) to the correct model before writing any code
- SSE-First Pattern — default to SSE for server-push use cases; upgrade to WebSockets only when bidirectionality is proven necessary
- Event Envelope Pattern — every event has {id, type, timestamp, payload}; the envelope is stable, the payload evolves per type
Anti pattern:
- hacer polling agresivo (cada 500ms) en vez de usar SSE/WS — desperdicia recursos, añade latencia y no escala.
- Long-polling in new agent systems — it is a workaround, not an architecture; SSE exists for this
- no manejar reconexión/backoff en el cliente — las conexiones WS se caen y el estudiante junior suele olvidar ese caso.
- Leaking internal agent state in the payload → couples the consumer to an implementation detail

  + Tiempo real en flujos agénticos con LangGraph:
    - Streaming modes de LangGraph (values, updates, messages, custom): esto es literalmente la aplicación práctica de la sección 2-3 (SSE/streaming vs batch) — el estudiante ya sabe qué es streaming, ahora ve cómo LangGraph expone distintos "niveles" de eventos.
    - Interrupciones y HITL (interrupt(), checkpointing): esto conecta directamente con el punto de WebSockets/bidireccionalidad — una interrupción real requiere que el cliente pueda "hablar de vuelta" mientras el grafo está pausado, no solo recibir tokens.
    - Comunicación entre nodos/agentes: aquí es donde Pub/Sub deja de ser abstracto — en sistemas multiagente con LangGraph, el paso de estado entre nodos y la comunicación agente-a-agente son una aplicación directa del patrón visto en la sección 4.
    - Checkpointing como mecanismo de persistencia del estado en tiempo real: útil para cerrar el círculo con tu currículo actual (checkpointing, memoria de agentes).
How to think:
- Explicar la diferencia entre SSE y WebSockets y cuándo usar cada uno.
- Reconocer cuándo un requisito ("el usuario debe poder interrumpir al agente") implica necesariamente un canal bidireccional.
- Use WebSockets only when the client must also send messages after the connection is open — collaborative editing, chat, agent interruption
- Client must not infer when the conversation or message finishes, it must be clear
- WebSockets es la moda y es poderoso, pero no debe ser escogido por eso sino porque la complejidad y la doble dirección de la comunicación lo requieren.
Best practices:
- Handle connection lifecycle explicitly: onopen, onmessage, onerror, onclose — all four, always

- Stream LLM output token by token via SSE from the backend — never buffer the full response before sending
- Separate the LLM API call from the HTTP response — the backend opens the LLM stream and pipes it directly into the SSE response
- Send a typed [DONE] event when the stream ends — the client must not infer completion from silence
- Use WebSocket or pub/sub for agent interruption — SSE is unidirectional; a user interrupting an agent mid-stream requires a back-channel

- Choose the streaming mode by consumer need: messages for token-level UI rendering, updates for step-level agent progress, values for full state inspection, custom for domain-specific events
- Use interrupt() before irreversible nodes — checkpointing must be configured for interrupt to be resumable
- Treat inter-node state passing as pub/sub — a node publishes its output to graph state; downstream nodes subscribe by reading their required keys
- Expose agent progress via custom stream events — do not force the frontend to parse updates to infer what the agent is doing
Patterns:
- Usar un backplane pub/sub (Redis) para escalar WebSockets horizontalmente — sin esto, sticky sessions se vuelven un cuello de botella.
- Message Envelope Pattern — {id, type, timestamp, payload} on every message; type drives client-side routing
- Heartbeat/Ping-Pong Pattern — server sends ping every 30s; client responds pong; server closes connection on missed responses
- Reconnect-with-Resume Pattern — client tracks last received message_id; sends it on reconnect so server can replay missed messages

- In pub/sub Publishers never know who is subscribed — if a publisher references a specific consumer, it is not pub/sub
- In pub/sub Use namespaced, hierarchical topic names — agent.{id}.token, task.{id}.completed, user.{id}.notification
- In pub/sub Keep payloads minimal and typed — the event tells what happened; the consumer fetches details if needed
- In pub/sub  Make every subscriber handler idempotent — the broker may deliver the same event more than once
- In pub/sub Define a dead letter topic for unprocessable events — never silently discard

- Pipe-Through Streaming Pattern — backend receives LLM chunks → immediately forwards each chunk as an SSE event → client renders token by token; no buffering at any layer
- Dual-Channel Pattern — SSE for server→client token stream; WebSocket back-channel for client→server interruptions and input during agent execution

- Stream-Mode-per-Consumer Pattern — UI token display → messages; progress indicator → updates; debug tooling → values; domain events → custom
- Checkpoint-then-Interrupt Pattern — checkpointer persists state → interrupt() pauses execution → WebSocket back-channel receives human input → resume() injects input into state and continues from checkpoint
- Node-as-Publisher Pattern — each node writes only to its declared state keys; downstream nodes read only their declared dependencies; graph state is the broker
Anti pattern:
- Awaiting the full LLM response before streaming — destroys perceived latency; the user waits for the slowest token

- No [DONE] event — client spinner hangs after the last token; UX breaks silently

- Using values mode for UI token streaming — sends full state snapshots on every node execution; expensive and noisy
- interrupt() without a configured checkpointer — the pause has nowhere to resume from; execution cannot continue
- Nodes reading keys they did not declare as dependencies — creates hidden coupling between agents that breaks when state schema evolves
- Inferring agent progress from updates parsing in the frontend — fragile; emit explicit custom events for consumer-facing progress signals

> Teoría: 

+ Gobierno de la IA:
  - Inventario de sistemas AI.
  - Responsabilidad de controles (¿quién es responsable de qué cuando el modelo lo provee un tercero?).
  - Introducción al marco regulatorio en Europa (EU AI Act, GDPR).
  - Introducción al marco regulatorio en América: FERPA y HIPAA

+ Principios de la seguridad por diseño:
  - Principios generales (aplicables a cualquier software)
    -- Least privilege: cada componente, API key o servicio debe tener solo los permisos mínimos necesarios.
    -- Defense in depth: no confiar en una sola capa de protección (validación en frontend Y backend, por ejemplo).
    -- Fail securely: si algo falla, debe fallar cerrado (denegando acceso), no abierto.
    -- Nunca confiar en el input del usuario: validar y sanitizar todo lo que entra al sistema.
    -- Secrets management: nunca hardcodear API keys o credenciales en el código; usar variables de entorno o vaults.
  - Riesgos específicos de aplicaciones con LLMs
    -- Prompt injection: el input del usuario puede intentar sobrescribir las instrucciones del sistema. Un junior debe entender la diferencia entre instrucciones de sistema y contenido de usuario, y por qué nunca se debe tratar el output de un LLM como código o comando confiable sin validación.
    -- Indirect prompt injection: cuando el LLM lee contenido externo (documentos, resultados de búsqueda, páginas web) que puede contener instrucciones maliciosas ocultas.
    -- Data leakage / exfiltración: evitar que información sensible (system prompts, datos de otros usuarios, secrets) termine en un output visible.
    -- Output validation: si el LLM genera código, SQL, o llamadas a herramientas, ese output debe tratarse como no confiable hasta validarse (evitar SQL injection generado por el propio modelo, por ejemplo).
    -- Excessive agency: cuando un agente tiene permisos para ejecutar acciones (tools, APIs, bash), hay que limitar el alcance de esas acciones y pedir confirmación humana en las irreversibles (borrar datos, enviar dinero, mandar emails).
  - Buenas prácticas concretas para ejercicios/proyectos
    -- Sandboxing de cualquier código generado o ejecutado por el modelo.
    -- Rate limiting y control de costos (evitar loops infinitos de llamadas a la API).
    -- Logging y trazabilidad de qué hizo el agente y por qué (auditoría).
    -- Human-in-the-loop para acciones sensibles.

+ NIST Security Checklist 
  - What is NIST and why is it important?
  - NIST function groups: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover
  - 🏛️ GOVERN (GV): Establishes organizational context, accountability, and risk strategy.
    -- Define organizational mission, risk appetite, and regulatory obligations
    -- Establish and communicate a cybersecurity policy endorsed by leadership
    -- Assign roles, responsibilities, and authority for cybersecurity decisions
    -- Integrate cybersecurity into enterprise risk management (ERM)
    -- Manage cybersecurity supply chain risks (third parties, vendors, suppliers)
    -- Maintain an ongoing cybersecurity awareness and workforce training program
    -- Review and update governance strategy periodically
  - 🔍 IDENTIFY (ID): Understand the organization's current cybersecurity risk exposure.
    -- Maintain an up-to-date inventory of hardware and software assets
    -- Identify data assets, their classification, and sensitivity
    -- Map business processes that depend on information systems
    -- Conduct and document risk assessments regularly
    -- Identify applicable legal, regulatory, and contractual cybersecurity requirements
    -- Assess vulnerabilities in systems and prioritize by criticality
  - 🛡️ PROTECT (PR): Implement safeguards to prevent or reduce cybersecurity risks.
    -- Enforce identity management and access control (least privilege, MFA)
    -- Apply security awareness training for all personnel
    -- Implement data security controls (encryption, data loss prevention)
    -- Establish secure configuration baselines for all systems
    -- Enable automatic patching and software updates
    -- Perform regular data backups and test recovery procedures
    -- Secure network infrastructure (segmentation, firewalls, VPNs)
    -- Manage physical security for facilities and devices
  - 📡 DETECT (DE): Identify cybersecurity events and anomalies in a timely manner.
    -- Deploy continuous monitoring across systems, networks, and assets
    -- Implement logging and audit trail capabilities
    -- Define and tune detection alerts for anomalous behavior
    -- Monitor for unauthorized access and insider threats
    -- Correlate threat intelligence with internal detection signals
    -- Test detection capabilities regularly (e.g., red team exercises)
  - 🚨 RESPOND (RS): Take action when a cybersecurity incident is detected.
    -- Develop and maintain an incident response plan (IRP)
    -- Define escalation paths and assign incident response roles
    -- Establish communication protocols (internal and external, including regulators)
    -- Contain incidents to prevent further damage
    -- Analyze incidents to determine root cause
    -- Document all response actions and decisions
    -- Coordinate with external parties if needed (law enforcement, CERTs)
  - ♻️ RECOVER (RC): Restore capabilities and services after a cybersecurity incident.
    -- Develop and test a recovery plan aligned with business continuity objectives
    -- Define recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO)
    -- Restore affected systems from validated backups
    -- Communicate recovery status to stakeholders
    -- Conduct post-incident review and update plans based on lessons learned
    -- Track improvements and validate that vulnerabilities are remediated
